title: Scientists filmed nature building penicillin, molecule by molecule
snippet: X-ray lasers captured the fleeting steps an enzyme uses to snap penicillin's ring together, solving a 40-year-old puzzle.
bullets: Oxford-led researchers used X-ray free-electron lasers to watch the enzyme IPNS at work.[1]
They caught a thioaldehyde intermediate and the first ring-shaped β-lactam stage before the full scaffold forms.[1]
It answers a mechanism question open for more than four decades and was published in Nature Catalysis in October 2026.[1]
report: Penicillin was turned into a medicine at Oxford in the 1940s, but how bacteria and fungi build its strained ring in one enzymatic step stayed murky.[1] The new 'molecular movie' shows the enzyme isopenicillin N synthase converting a straight chain peptide into the ring system.[1]
Understanding the steps could help chemists design new antibiotic scaffolds as resistance grows. Penicillin itself was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928.[2]
qa: Isopenicillin N synthase, the enzyme that turns a linear peptide into penicillin's two-ring core in one step.
Seeing each step could help design new antibiotics as bacteria grow resistant.

sources.title: Ingenious 'molecular movie' finally reveals how penicillin is made | Oxford University

image.credit: Science Museum London / Science and Society Picture Library

title: A single speck of antimatter was held still for months
snippet: Northwestern physicists trapped one positron, cooled it to its quantum ground state, and kept it for months.
bullets: A positron (the electron's antimatter twin) was held in a Penning trap with electric and magnetic fields.[1]
Cooled to about 0.3 K, it settled into its quantum ground state and was kept for months.[1]
Goal: compare matter and antimatter magnetism to test CPT symmetry with extreme precision.[1]
report: Antimatter usually annihilates the instant it touches normal matter, which is why holding one particle for months is remarkable.[1] The same group previously measured the electron's magnetic moment to about one part in 10 trillion.[1]
A Penning trap uses a strong uniform magnetic field and an electric quadrupole field to confine charged particles.[2]
qa: The antimatter counterpart of the electron: same mass, opposite (positive) charge.
The idea that physics looks the same if you flip charge, mirror space and reverse time, so particles and antiparticles should have identical magnetism apart from sign.

sources.title: Science news in review: Oct. 26 - The Johns Hopkins News-Letter

title: Perseverance just set an off-world driving record
snippet: NASA's Mars rover broke a driving record on 21 October 2026, helped by its self-driving system.
bullets: Perseverance set an off-world driving record on 21 October 2026.[1]
Its autonomous navigation (AutoNav) lets it plan paths without waiting for Earth.[2]
It has been exploring Jezero Crater since landing on 18 February 2021.[2]
report: Radio signals take several minutes each way between Earth and Mars, so a rover that thinks for itself covers far more ground.[2] Perseverance is collecting rock cores that may one day be returned to Earth.[2]
Weekly roundups flagged the record alongside new Curiosity images of wind-carved cliffs.[1]
qa: It builds 3D maps from its cameras and picks safe paths on the fly (AutoNav).
Jezero Crater, an ancient lake bed on Mars.

sources.title: This week in science, 20–26 October | Your Daily Science

title: A giant underwater volcano in Japan is quietly refilling
snippet: Kikai caldera, site of a huge eruption 7,300 years ago, is refilling with magma.
bullets: Researchers report the Kikai caldera south of Kyushu is refilling with magma.[1]
Its eruption about 7,300 years ago was one of the largest of the Holocene.[2]
Refilling is slow and doesn't mean an eruption is imminent.[1]
report: The Kikai-Akahoya eruption spread ash across southern Japan and is thought to have badly hit the Jōmon people of Kyushu.[2]
Most of the caldera is underwater; Satsuma Iōjima island is part of its rim.[2]
qa: No. The reports describe slow refilling over a long time, not a warning.
Off southern Kyushu, Japan, mostly underwater.

sources.title: This week in science, 20–26 October | Your Daily Science

title: Wombats poop cubes. Physics explains how
snippet: The only animal known to make cube-shaped droppings, thanks to stretchy gut walls.
bullets: Bare-nosed wombats produce cube-shaped faeces, up to around 100 a night.[1]
Varying elasticity in the last part of the intestine shapes the corners.[2]
The research won a 2019 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics.[2]
report: Wombats use their droppings to mark territory, often on rocks and logs, where cubes don't roll away.[1]
Researchers at Georgia Tech found stiffer and more flexible regions of the gut wall sculpt flat sides and sharp corners.[2]
qa: Cubes stay put on rocks and logs, useful for marking territory.
Uneven stretchiness in the intestine wall forms flat sides and corners.

title: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood
snippet: Two hearts pump blood to the gills, one to the body, and copper makes it blue.
bullets: Octopuses have three hearts: two branchial and one systemic.[1]
Their blood uses copper-rich hemocyanin, which turns it blue.[1]
Most of their neurons are in their arms.[1]
report: The systemic heart actually stops beating while an octopus swims, one reason they prefer crawling.[1]
Hemocyanin carries oxygen well in cold, low-oxygen water.[1]
qa: They use copper-based hemocyanin instead of iron-based hemoglobin.
Very. They solve puzzles and use tools like coconut shells.

title: Honey basically never goes bad
snippet: Low water, high acidity and a built-in hydrogen peroxide trick make honey last for ages.
bullets: Honey's low water activity stops most microbes from growing.[1]
Bees add the enzyme glucose oxidase, which produces hydrogen peroxide.[1]
Stored sealed, it can last indefinitely, though it may crystallise.[1]
report: Crystallised honey isn't spoiled: warm the jar gently and it turns liquid again.[1]
Honey's high sugar content draws water out of microbes by osmosis.[1]
qa: Only if it absorbs water and ferments. Kept sealed, it lasts.
Glucose comes out of solution. It's harmless.

title: Tardigrades survived the vacuum of space
snippet: These half-millimetre 'water bears' can dry out and come back to life.
bullets: Tardigrades are micro-animals, usually under 1 mm long.[1]
In 2007 some survived exposure to open space on the FOTON-M3 mission.[1]
They survive by entering a dried-out 'tun' state (cryptobiosis).[1]
report: They live almost everywhere: moss, lichens, sea floors and Antarctic ice.[1]
In the tun state their metabolism drops to under 0.01% of normal.[1]
qa: Soak some moss in water and look with a cheap microscope.
No, but they're among the toughest animals known.

title: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire
snippet: Teaching at Oxford began by 1096. Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325.
bullets: There is evidence of teaching at Oxford as early as 1096.[1]
The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan around 1325.[2]
History's timelines overlap in ways that feel wrong.[1][2]
report: Oxford grew quickly after 1167 when Henry II banned English students from attending the University of Paris.[1]
The Aztec Triple Alliance formed in 1428.[2]
qa: Yes: Oxford ~1096; Tenochtitlan 1325; Aztec Triple Alliance 1428.

title: Bananas are slightly radioactive
snippet: They contain potassium-40, which is why scientists joke about the 'banana equivalent dose'.
bullets: Bananas contain potassium, including tiny amounts of radioactive potassium-40.[1]
The 'banana equivalent dose' is an informal way to explain radiation.[1]
Eating one is harmless: your body keeps potassium levels steady.[1]
report: One banana dose is often quoted as about 0.1 microsieverts.[1]
You'd get far more from a cross-country flight.[1]
qa: No. The dose is tiny and your body regulates potassium.

title: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the Great Pyramid
snippet: The Great Pyramid was ~2,500 years old when Cleopatra was born.
bullets: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BC.[1]
Cleopatra VII lived 69–30 BC.[2]
Apollo 11 landed in 1969, about 2,000 years after her.[2]
report: The pyramid was the tallest human-made structure for over 3,800 years.[1]
Ancient Egypt lasted so long that it had its own 'ancient history'.[1]
qa: Pyramid ~2560 BC to Cleopatra ~69 BC is ~2,490 years; Cleopatra to 1969 is ~2,040 years.

title: Sharks are older than trees
snippet: Sharks appeared ~450 million years ago; the first trees ~385 million years ago.
bullets: The earliest shark-like fish date to about 450 million years ago.[1]
The earliest known trees (like Archaeopteris & Wattieza) appeared ~385 million years ago.[2]
Sharks have survived all five big mass extinctions.[1]
report: Sharks also predate Saturn's rings by some estimates.[1]
Archaeopteris forests changed Earth's soils and atmosphere.[2]
qa: Wattieza and Archaeopteris are among the earliest known.

title: A day on Venus is longer than its year
snippet: Venus spins so slowly that one rotation takes longer than one orbit around the Sun.
bullets: Venus rotates once every ~243 Earth days.[1]
It orbits the Sun every ~225 Earth days.[1]
It also spins backwards compared with most planets.[1]
report: Its surface is ~465 °C, hotter than Mercury, because of a runaway greenhouse effect.[1]
Soviet Venera landers sent back the only photos from its surface.[1]
qa: Possibly a giant impact or tidal effects from its thick atmosphere.

title: The Eiffel Tower grows in summer
snippet: Heat makes its iron expand by up to around 15 cm.
bullets: The Eiffel Tower is made of wrought (puddled) iron.[1]
Thermal expansion can make it grow roughly 15 cm on hot days.[1]
It was built for the 1889 World's Fair and was meant to be temporary.[1]
report: It was the world's tallest structure until the Chrysler Building in 1930.[1]
It's repainted about every seven years.[1]
qa: Metal expands when heated: thermal expansion.

title: Lightning can turn sand into glass
snippet: When lightning hits sand it can fuse it into hollow glass tubes called fulgurites.
bullets: Fulgurites form when lightning melts silica sand or rock.[1]
They're often hollow, branching tubes.[1]
Temperatures can exceed 1,800 °C in an instant.[1]
report: Fulgurites can also form on rock surfaces as glassy crusts.[1]
qa: Sometimes, on sandy beaches or deserts after storms.

title: The mantis shrimp punches like a bullet
snippet: Its club strikes so fast it boils the water around it.
bullets: Peacock mantis shrimp strike with accelerations comparable to a .22 bullet.[1]
The strike creates cavitation bubbles that collapse with a flash and heat.[1]
They can break aquarium glass.[1]
report: Their eyes have 12–16 photoreceptor types, compared with our three.[1]
qa: Large ones have cracked aquarium glass.

title: A blue whale's heart is the size of a small car
snippet: The largest animal ever known has a heart weighing around 180 kg.
bullets: Blue whales can reach about 30 m long.[1]
Their hearts have been measured at ~180 kg.[1]
They're the largest animals known to have ever lived.[1]
report: They eat up to around 3.6 tonnes of krill a day.[1]
qa: Yes, by mass blue whales beat any known dinosaur.

title: A tiny dark patch of sky held 3,000 galaxies
snippet: Hubble stared at an 'empty' speck for 10 days and found thousands of galaxies.
bullets: The Hubble Deep Field (1995) covered a patch about 1/24 millionth of the sky.[1]
It revealed about 3,000 galaxies.[1]
It changed estimates of how many galaxies exist.[1]
report: Follow-ups like the Ultra Deep Field went even deeper.[1]
qa: Like a tennis ball seen from 100 m away.

title: Australia once lost a 'war' to emus
snippet: In 1932 soldiers with machine guns took on 20,000 emus. The emus won.
bullets: In 1932 Australia deployed soldiers with Lewis guns against emus in Western Australia.[1]
The birds scattered into small groups and proved very hard to hit.[1]
The operation was widely mocked and withdrawn.[1]
report: Major G.P.W. Meredith reportedly compared the emus to tanks for their ability to take damage.[1]
Farmers later turned to bounty systems and fencing.[1]
qa: The military withdrew after limited success, so the emus are usually declared the winners.

title: London's smell was so bad Parliament had to fix it
snippet: The 'Great Stink' of 1858 finally got London its modern sewer system.
bullets: In the hot summer of 1858, sewage in the Thames created an overwhelming stench.[1]
MPs soaked curtains in chloride of lime to cope.[1]
It led to Joseph Bazalgette's sewer network.[1]
report: The sewers also helped end cholera outbreaks in London.[1]
qa: Bazalgette's sewer system, much still in use today.

title: A cat was honorary mayor of an Alaska town for 20 years
snippet: Stubbs the cat 'ran' Talkeetna from 1997 to 2017.
bullets: Stubbs was the honorary mayor of Talkeetna, Alaska.[1]
He 'held office' for about 20 years.[1]
Tourists visited his general store office.[1]
report: Talkeetna has no actual human mayor, which made the role easy to keep.[1]
qa: Honorary. Talkeetna is a census area with no mayor.

title: Napoleon was once ambushed by rabbits
snippet: A hunt went wrong when hundreds of tame rabbits charged him, by legend.
bullets: A popular story says a rabbit hunt arranged for Napoleon went awry in 1807.[1]
Tame rabbits supposedly swarmed him instead of fleeing.[1]
The tale is widely repeated but comes from memoir, not solid records.[1]
report: Treat it as a fun legend: the main source is the memoirs of General Thiébault.[1]
qa: It's from memoirs and can't be verified. Fun legend, use with a wink.

title: A penguin is a knight in the Norwegian army
snippet: Sir Nils Olav III, king penguin at Edinburgh Zoo, holds the rank of Major General.
bullets: Nils Olav is the mascot of the Norwegian King's Guard.[1]
He was knighted in 2008 and promoted to brigadier and later major general.[1]
He lives at Edinburgh Zoo.[1]
report: There's a bronze statue of him at the zoo.[1]
qa: Yes, a ceremonial title from the Norwegian King's Guard.

title: The internet voted to name a ship 'Boaty McBoatface'
snippet: The UK named the ship after Attenborough, but a sub got the name.
bullets: A 2016 online poll to name a UK polar research ship picked 'Boaty McBoatface'.[1]
The ship became RRS Sir David Attenborough.[1]
An autonomous submarine on board got the Boaty name.[1]
report: Boaty the sub has since explored deep Antarctic waters.[1]
qa: Still used as an autonomous underwater vehicle for research.

title: A jet ran out of fuel because of a unit mix-up, then glided to safety
snippet: In 1983 an Air Canada 767 was fuelled in pounds instead of kilograms.
bullets: Air Canada Flight 143 ran out of fuel at 41,000 feet in 1983.[1]
The cause: a fuel calculation using pounds instead of kilograms.[1]
The captain, a glider pilot, landed it at a former airbase in Gimli.[1]
report: Nobody died; the plane flew again until 2008.[1]
qa: The captain used a gliding technique called a forward slip to lose height.

title: Sea otters hold hands while they sleep
snippet: So they don't drift apart. Some also wrap themselves in kelp.
bullets: Sea otters float in groups called rafts.[1]
They sometimes hold paws or wrap in kelp to avoid drifting.[1]
They have the densest fur of any animal.[1]
report: Up to around a million hairs per square inch keep them warm.[1]
qa: It anchors them so they don't drift away while sleeping.

image.credit: Mike Baird from Morro Bay, USA

title: Crows remember your face and hold grudges
snippet: Researchers in masks found crows scolded the 'villain' mask for years.
bullets: University of Washington researchers trapped crows while wearing a mask.[1]
Crows later scolded that mask, even birds that weren't trapped.[1]
Crows are among the most intelligent birds.[1]
report: The New Caledonian crow even makes hooked tools.[1]
qa: They can learn friendly faces as well.

title: Everyone who ever lived is on one pixel
snippet: In 1990 Voyager 1 looked back from 6 billion km and saw Earth as a pale blue dot.
bullets: Voyager 1 took the Pale Blue Dot photo on 14 February 1990.[1]
Earth was less than one pixel in size.[1]
Carl Sagan's reflection on it became famous.[1]
report: Sagan used it to argue for kindness and protecting our only home.[1]

title: 1% better a day is 37x better in a year
snippet: Small improvements compound. 1.01^365 ≈ 37.8.
bullets: Compounding means gains build on previous gains.[1]
It's a metaphor, not a law of personal growth, but the direction holds.[1]
report: The same math powers investing over decades.[1]
qa: It's a metaphor. Real progress is lumpy, but small habits do add up.

title: If you replace every plank, is it the same ship?
snippet: The Ship of Theseus puzzle, and your body replaces many cells too.
bullets: Plutarch described the Athenians replacing Theseus's ship plank by plank.[1]
Philosophers still debate what makes identity persist.[1]
Many of your cells are replaced over time, though not all.[1]
report: Hobbes added a twist: what if the old planks were rebuilt into a second ship?[1]
qa: There isn't one agreed answer; it depends on what you think identity is.

title: Astronauts come back changed: the Overview Effect
snippet: Seeing Earth from space triggers awe and a sense of connection.
bullets: Coined by Frank White in 1987.[1]
Astronauts describe a cognitive shift on seeing Earth as a whole.[1]
Borders become invisible from orbit.[1]
report: Researchers study whether VR can recreate some of the effect.[1]

title: The less we know, the more confident we can feel
snippet: The Dunning–Kruger effect describes over-confidence at low skill.
bullets: David Dunning and Justin Kruger described it in 1999.[1]
Low performers often overestimate their ability.[1]
Some researchers argue part of it is a statistical artifact.[1]
report: The useful takeaway: confidence isn't evidence.[1]
qa: The pattern is debated; part may be statistical noise. The humility lesson still stands.

title: 25 minutes. One task. Then a break.
snippet: The Pomodoro Technique turns big tasks into tiny sprints.
bullets: Created by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s using a tomato kitchen timer.[1]
Work 25 minutes, break 5; longer break after four rounds.[1]
Short timers help when starting is the hard part.[1]
report: Pomodoro is Italian for tomato.[1]
qa: Try 10 or 15. The point is starting, not the number.

title: If it takes under 2 minutes, do it now
snippet: David Allen's two-minute rule clears small stuff before it piles up.
bullets: From David Allen's Getting Things Done (2001).[1]
If an action takes under two minutes, doing it beats tracking it.[1]
Great for emails, dishes, quick replies.[1]
report: GTD's core idea: get tasks out of your head into a trusted system.[1]
qa: Pick one thing that takes under 2 minutes and do it before the next card.

title: Walking boosts creative thinking
snippet: A Stanford study found walking increased creative output by about 60%.
bullets: Stanford researchers Oppezzo & Schwartz (2014) tested walking vs sitting.[1]
Walking boosted creative idea generation substantially.[1]
Effects carried over briefly after the walk.[1]
report: Nietzsche said 'all truly great thoughts are conceived while walking'.[1]
qa: Even short walks of 5-15 minutes helped in the study.

sources.title: Stanford study finds walking improves creativity | Stanford Report

title: Sleep is when your brain files your memories
snippet: During sleep, the brain replays and consolidates what you learned.
bullets: Sleep plays a role in memory consolidation.[1]
Deep sleep and REM support different memory types.[1]
Adults generally need 7+ hours.[2]
report: A short nap can help too.[1]
qa: CDC recommends 7 or more hours for adults.

title: Splash cold water on your face to calm down fast
snippet: The diving reflex slows your heart rate in seconds.
bullets: Cold water on the face triggers the mammalian diving reflex.[1]
It slows heart rate (bradycardia).[1]
It's a quick, safe reset for many people.[1]
report: The reflex is stronger in colder water.[1]
qa: Generally, but people with heart conditions should check with a doctor.

title: Box breathing: 4 in, 4 hold, 4 out, 4 hold
snippet: Slow breathing activates the body's 'rest and digest' mode.
bullets: Breathe in 4s, hold 4s, out 4s, hold 4s; repeat.[1]
Slow breathing can increase heart-rate variability and calm.[1]
Used by athletes and first responders.[1]
report: Try 4 rounds right now.[1]

title: Japan prescribes 'forest bathing'
snippet: Shinrin-yoku: slow walks among trees to reduce stress.
bullets: Shinrin-yoku was promoted in Japan from the 1980s.[1]
Studies link it to lower stress markers.[1]
No exercise needed: just slow, attentive time among trees.[1]
report: Even looking at nature photos may help a little.[1]
qa: A park or tree-lined street counts.

title: Why the sky dances green
snippet: Auroras happen when solar particles hit oxygen and nitrogen high above Earth.
bullets: Charged solar particles follow Earth's magnetic field to the poles.[1]
Oxygen glows green (~100-300 km) and red higher up.[1]
Nitrogen adds blues and purples.[1]
report: 2024's strong solar storms brought auroras unusually far south.[1]
qa: Dark, clear nights near the poles, during high solar activity.

image.credit: United States Air Force photo by Senior Airman Joshua Strang

title: Glowing waves are made of tiny plankton
snippet: Dinoflagellates flash blue when water moves.
bullets: Bioluminescent dinoflagellates light up when disturbed.[1]
The blue glow comes from luciferin reacting with luciferase.[1]
Seen on beaches worldwide during blooms.[1]
report: The flash may startle predators.[1]
qa: Places like Puerto Rico's Mosquito Bay or Maldives beaches during blooms.

title: Why cats purr (it's not just happiness)
snippet: Cats purr when content, but also when stressed or healing.
bullets: Purring is produced by the laryngeal muscles.[1]
Cats purr at about 25-150 Hz.[1]
They also purr when hurt or anxious.[1]
report: Some suggest purr frequencies help healing; evidence is limited.[1]
qa: Cheetahs and some others do; lions and tigers roar instead.

title: Mount Everest is still growing
snippet: Tectonic forces lift the Himalayas a few millimetres a year.
bullets: The Indian plate is still pushing into Asia.[1]
Everest's official height is 8,848.86 m (2020).[1]
A 2024 study suggested river erosion adds extra uplift.[1]
report: Everest's summit rock was once seafloor: it has marine fossils.[1]

title: Saturn would float in water
snippet: It's less dense than water, if you could find a big enough bathtub.
bullets: Saturn's average density is ~0.69 g/cm³; water is 1.[1]
It's mostly hydrogen and helium.[1]
Its rings are mostly ice.[1]
report: The rings are only about 10 m thick in places.[1]
qa: In theory, yes, on average density alone.

image.credit: NASA / JPL-Caltech / SSI / color composite by Gordan Ugarkovic

title: Trees share resources through fungal networks
snippet: Mycorrhizal networks link roots, though the 'Wood Wide Web' is debated.
bullets: Mycorrhizal fungi connect with plant roots.[1]
They exchange nutrients for sugars.[1]
Claims of trees deliberately 'helping' each other are contested.[1]
report: A 2023 review urged caution about popular claims.[1]
qa: They connect via fungi, but deliberate 'talking' is overstated.

image.credit: Світлана Шахнович, КНУТД, керівник Євгенія Романюк

title: We sent a mixtape to aliens
snippet: Voyager's Golden Records carry sounds and music from Earth.
bullets: Launched in 1977 on Voyager 1 and 2.[1]
Includes greetings in 55 languages, music and natural sounds.[1]
Curated by a committee chaired by Carl Sagan.[1]
report: It includes Chuck Berry's 'Johnny B. Goode'.[1]
qa: Voyager 1 is in interstellar space, over 24 billion km away.

title: A 1958 LEGO brick still fits today's bricks
snippet: Same clutch system for over 60 years.
bullets: LEGO patented its stud-and-tube brick in 1958.[1]
Modern bricks still connect with 1958 bricks.[1]
Tolerances are tiny, to a few micrometres.[1]
report: LEGO comes from Danish 'leg godt', 'play well'.[1]
